title: Volume and liquidity
teaches: Read volume: shares traded, the average day and dollar volume, then tell a liquid stock from a thin one and see why thin names cost you on the way in and the way out.

facts.quote: This is the daily number of shares of a security that change hands between a buyer and a seller.
facts.claim: Volume is the number of a stock's shares that change hands in a day.

facts.quote: As there is a seller for every buyer, one can think of the trading volume as half of the number of shares transacted.
facts.claim: Every share traded has a buyer and a seller, and volume counts that share once.

facts.quote: That is, if A sells 100 shares to B, the volume is 100 shares.
facts.claim: When one investor sells 100 shares to another, volume is 100 shares, not 200.

facts.quote: Remember that a unit of volume represents a transaction of a buyer and seller. If you want to buy a stock, you have to find a seller.
facts.claim: Every share of volume has a buyer and a seller; to buy, you have to find a seller.

facts.quote: Volume is simply the number of shares traded in a particular stock or other investment over a specific period of time.
facts.claim: Volume is the number of shares traded over a set period.

facts.quote: You can tell when volume is high or low by comparing the current level to another time period (such as previous days, weeks, or months, depending on your time frame), an average, or some other benchmark.
facts.claim: You judge volume as high or low by comparing it with past periods or with an average.

facts.quote: Consider the chart below where the top half shows the daily price of the S&P 500 and the bottom half shows the corresponding daily volume.
facts.claim: Fidelity's example chart shows daily price in the top half and daily volume in the bottom half.

facts.quote: The Average Volume is the total volume for a specified period divided by the number of bars in that same period.
facts.claim: Average volume is the total volume over a period divided by the number of bars in it.

facts.quote: Compare the Average Volume for the specified period to determine if volume is above or below average.
facts.claim: Compare a day's volume with the average to see whether it is above or below normal.

facts.quote: ADTV means the average daily trading volume reported for the security during the four calendar weeks preceding the week in which the Rule 10b-18 purchase is to be effected.
facts.claim: The SEC's buyback rule measures average daily trading volume (ADTV) as the daily average over the prior four calendar weeks.

facts.quote: Average daily trading volume (ADTV) is a measure of the average total shares traded for a stock each day during a specific time frame, providing insight into its liquidity and investor interest.
facts.claim: Average daily volume is the average number of shares traded per day over a set time frame, and it gives a read on liquidity.

facts.quote: Higher ADTV generally suggests greater liquidity, allowing easier entry and exit from positions without impacting the market price significantly.
facts.claim: Higher average volume usually means easier entries and exits without moving the price much.

facts.quote: If the ADTV is low, it suggests that the security may be less actively traded, and small buy or sell orders can have a larger impact on the price.
facts.claim: When average volume is low, even small orders can move the price more.

facts.quote: Traders often use ADTV as a benchmark for determining appropriate trade sizes.
facts.claim: Traders often use average daily volume as a benchmark for how big a trade should be.

facts.quote: On any given day an asset can deviate from the average, producing much higher or lower volume.
facts.claim: Any single day can trade far above or far below the average.

facts.quote: Significant volume changes can indicate shifting investor interest, though ADTV itself does not predict direction.
facts.claim: Big changes in volume can signal shifting interest, but average volume does not predict direction.

facts.quote: A stock’s liquidity generally refers to how rapidly shares of a stock can be bought or sold without substantially impacting the stock price.
facts.claim: A stock is liquid when its shares can be bought or sold quickly without a big move in the price.

facts.quote: Stocks with low liquidity may be difficult to sell and may cause you to take a bigger loss if you cannot sell the shares when you want to.
facts.claim: Illiquid stocks can be hard to sell, and that can turn into a bigger loss.

facts.quote: When it comes to securities investing, market liquidity refers to how easily you can buy or sell an investment at a fair market price when you want to.
facts.claim: Market liquidity is how easily you can buy or sell at a fair price when you want to.

facts.quote: You might have to accept a lower price if you need to sell quickly.
facts.claim: Selling an illiquid stock fast can mean taking a lower price.

facts.quote: In some cases, you might not be able to sell at all if no one is willing to buy at a price you’re willing to accept.
facts.claim: Sometimes there is no buyer at any price you would accept.

facts.quote: If you want to buy an illiquid security, you might have to pay a higher price or wait longer to find a seller.
facts.claim: Buying an illiquid stock can mean paying up or waiting for a seller.

facts.quote: Generally, securities with higher trading volume are more liquid. Executing a large order quickly in a low-volume security can be difficult.
facts.claim: Higher volume usually means more liquid, and a large order in a low-volume stock is hard to fill quickly.

facts.quote: A narrow spread can indicate good liquidity but doesn’t provide a complete picture on its own.
facts.claim: A tight spread hints at liquidity but is not the whole picture.

facts.quote: Large-cap stocks are usually more liquid than small- or micro-cap stocks.
facts.claim: Large-cap stocks are usually more liquid than small-cap or micro-cap stocks.

facts.quote: For example, well-known stocks with higher daily trading volumes are generally more liquid than low-priced, low-volume or obscure securities.
facts.claim: Well-known stocks with heavy daily volume are generally more liquid than cheap, low-volume or obscure ones.

facts.quote: During times of crisis or market volatility, investors often seek lower-risk assets. This might drive interest in the most liquid securities, while illiquid investments might become even less liquid.
facts.claim: In a crisis, money moves to the most liquid names, and illiquid ones can become even less liquid.

facts.quote: They prevent you from accepting an unwanted price when trading in illiquid markets. However, a limit order might sit unfilled if there aren’t enough buyers or sellers at your specified price or better.
facts.claim: Limit orders keep you from taking an unwanted price in an illiquid market, but they may not fill.

facts.quote: They tend to be volatile, and they trade in low volumes, which means they’re subject to price fluctuations from even relatively small trades.
facts.claim: Low-priced stocks often trade in low volumes, so even fairly small trades can move their price.

facts.quote: The low trading volume of these securities also can make them hard to sell due to a potential lack of buyers.
facts.claim: Low trading volume can make a stock hard to sell because buyers may not be there.

facts.quote: The potential combination of minimal information and low trading volume can also make it easier for bad actors to manipulate an OTC stock’s price to their advantage.
facts.claim: Little public information plus low trading volume makes an OTC stock's price easier to manipulate.

facts.quote: bad actors might exploit the sense of safety that comes from exchange-listed stocks and target these securities for manipulation schemes, particularly stocks that that have low trading volume and trade at a lower price ($5 or less)
facts.claim: Bad actors target exchange-listed stocks too, particularly ones with low trading volume and a price of $5 or less.

facts.quote: treat stocks with a small market cap, foreign issuers or significant price spikes and drops with particular caution.
facts.claim: FINRA says to treat small caps and stocks with sharp price spikes and drops with particular caution.

facts.quote: Another risk that pertains to microcap stocks involves the low volumes of trades, which may make it difficult for you to sell your shares when you want to do so.
facts.claim: Low volume can make it hard to sell your shares when you want to.

facts.quote: Because many microcap stocks trade in low volumes, any size trade can have a large percentage impact on the price of the stock.
facts.claim: In a low-volume stock, any size trade can move the price a lot in percentage terms.

facts.quote: In addition, parts of a large market order may execute at different prices due to lack of liquidity at a price at the time of execution.
facts.claim: When one price lacks enough shares, parts of a big market order can fill at other prices.

facts.quote: The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop order becomes a market order once its stop price is hit.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the demand for a stock and the prices of available liquidity.
facts.claim: Once a stop triggers, the fill can land far from the stop price, depending on the liquidity there.

facts.quote: A security must have a three-month average daily value traded (“ADVT”) of at least $5 million (USD).
facts.claim: Nasdaq's current Nasdaq-100 rule measures liquidity in dollars: at least $5 million traded a day, on a three-month average.

facts.quote: The Nasdaq-100 Index methodology, as currently written, requires a security to have a minimum average daily trading volume of 200,000 shares.
facts.claim: In November 2023 the Nasdaq-100 liquidity test was an average of 200,000 shares traded a day.

facts.quote: In terms of dollar volume, this imposes a more stringent requirement on companies with higher stock prices and a less stringent requirement on those with lower prices.
facts.claim: Measured in dollars, a share-count test is tougher on high-priced stocks and easier on cheap ones.

facts.quote: Recent prices of current NDX members range from as little as $5 per share, to as high as $2,800.
facts.claim: Nasdaq-100 members then ranged from about $5 to $2,800 a share.

facts.quote: annual dollar value traded is defined as the average closing price multiplied by the historical volume over the 365 calendar days prior to the evaluation date.
facts.claim: S&P Dow Jones Indices measures dollar value traded as price times volume.

facts.quote: Volume is the number of shares that trade on any given day. The higher the volume, the better.
facts.claim: Volume is the shares traded in a day, and more volume makes a stock easier to trade.

facts.quote: For example, if JKL trades, on average, 10 million shares per day, it will be easier to trade than something that trades 100 shares per day.
facts.claim: A stock that trades millions of shares a day is easier to trade than one that trades a handful.

facts.quote: If you try to buy 10,000 shares of something that only trades 100 shares per day, you could have trouble.
facts.claim: An order far bigger than a stock's daily volume can run into trouble.

facts.quote: All else equal, you will do better trading something that has high volume and a tight bid/ask spread.
facts.claim: You do better trading names with both high volume and a tight spread.

facts.quote: where even small orders have the potential to represent a high percentage of an ETF's average daily volume and, as a result, impact the prevailing market price.
facts.claim: In thinly traded names, even a small order can be a big share of average daily volume and move the price.

facts.quote: Trading volume, which measures the number of shares traded during a particular time period
facts.claim: Trading volume measures the number of shares traded during a period.

facts.quote: “Liquidity” is broadly defined as the relative ease with which a security can be bought or sold without impacting its price.
facts.claim: Liquidity is how easily a security can be bought or sold without moving its price.

facts.quote: High trading volumes and narrow spreads indicate that a stock can be bought or sold in significant volume without impacting (or moving) its price.
facts.claim: High volume and narrow spreads mean a stock can take size without its price moving.

facts.quote: For this reason, average daily trading volume is generally a clear indicator of stock liquidity.
facts.claim: For a stock, average daily volume is generally a clear sign of how liquid it is.

facts.quote: If volume so far today is above or below average, it's helpful to know for a sense of how much conviction a move might have.
facts.claim: Knowing whether today's volume is above or below average gives a sense of how much conviction a move might have.

facts.quote: Volume can be plotted in an 'indicator panel' above or below the 'price plot area' or in the price plot area as an 'overlay.'
facts.claim: Charts show volume in its own panel near the price, or laid over the price area.

facts.quote: A volume spike is usually seen on earnings or some 'report' or environmental change that moves traders into the emotional zone and they trade accordingly.
facts.claim: Volume spikes usually come on earnings, reports or news.

facts.quote: Extended-hours trading might offer less liquidity because fewer transactions occur outside regular trading hours, resulting in fewer buyers or sellers available to take the opposite side of your trade.
facts.claim: Outside regular hours there are fewer buyers and sellers, so liquidity is lower.

facts.quote: The total value of a company’s outstanding shares of stock is referred to as market capitalization, or market cap.
facts.claim: Market cap is the total value of a company's outstanding shares.

facts.quote: the last-traded price is not necessarily the price at which a market order will be executed.
facts.claim: The last trade is not the price your market order is promised.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: Our rule: we trade only stocks priced at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and we do not even watch illiquid stocks.

walkthroughs.title: What volume counts
steps: Volume is the number of shares that change hands.
Many charts show price on top and volume in a pane below. On a daily chart, each bar is one day.
Every share traded has a buyer and a seller. If A sells 100 shares to B, that's 100 shares of volume.

walkthroughs.title: The normal day, in dollars
steps: Any one day can run far above or below normal. So read the average first.
Average volume is the total over a stretch of days, divided by the number of days.
Then multiply by the price. That's dollar volume, roughly the money that changes hands.

walkthroughs.title: Why thin names hurt
steps: A liquid stock lets you buy and sell fast without moving the price much.
A thin one doesn't. Even small orders can push the price around.
When you need out fast, you may have to take a lower price. Sometimes there's no buyer at your price at all.

questions.q: On a daily chart, what does a stock's volume tell you?
questions.why: Shares traded that day. Volume is the daily number of shares that change hands between a buyer and a seller. It counts shares, not trades, so one big trade can add a lot of shares. It says how much traded, not how far the price moved or how many shares the company has.
questions.lesson_line: Volume counts the shares that changed hands. On a daily chart, each volume bar is one day.

wrong.Number of trades placed: Volume counts shares, not trades. One big trade can add a lot of shares.
wrong.Shares the company has issued: That's the company's share count, not its trading. Volume is only the shares that traded.
wrong.How far the price moved: That's the day's range or change. Volume says how much traded, not how far price went.

questions.simple: Volume is the number of shares that changed hands that day, not the number of trades.

reasons: fixed before (q01 wrong-note on issued shares)

questions.q: When one investor sells 100 shares to another, the day's volume goes up by 200 shares.
questions.why: False. Volume counts each traded share once. If A sells 100 shares to B, the volume is 100 shares, not 200. Nasdaq's glossary says it another way. With a seller for every buyer, volume is half the shares counted on both sides.
questions.lesson_line: Every share traded has a buyer and a seller. Volume counts it once.
questions.simple: False, because each share sold to a buyer counts once, so 100 shares sold adds 100 to volume.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Add up a stock's volume over a stretch of days and divide by the number of days. That's its ___ volume.
questions.why: Average. The total volume for a period, divided by the number of bars in it, is the average volume. The period is a choice: the SEC's buyback rule, for example, uses the prior four calendar weeks. Total is the sum before you divide.
questions.lesson_line: The average tells you what a normal day looks like for this stock.
questions.simple: It is the average volume, because you add up the days and divide by how many days there are.

questions.q: Which kind of stock is usually the easiest to buy and sell quickly?
questions.why: A large-cap stock. FINRA says large caps are usually more liquid than small or micro caps. Well-known stocks with heavy daily volume are generally more liquid than low-priced, low-volume or obscure ones. Usually is the key word: stocks with higher trading volume are generally more liquid, so check the volume itself.
questions.lesson_line: Big, heavily traded names are usually the easiest to get in and out of.

wrong.A small-cap: Small caps are usually less liquid than large caps, so getting in and out quickly can be harder.
wrong.A micro-cap: Micro caps often trade in low volumes. Even small trades can move them, and selling can be hard.
wrong.A cheap stock: A low price is not liquidity. Low-priced stocks tend to trade in low volumes, so even fairly small trades can move them.

questions.simple: A large-cap stock, because FINRA says large caps are usually more liquid than small or micro caps.

questions.q: When we call a stock liquid, what do we mean?
choices: Easy to trade without moving the price
The company holds plenty of cash
Its price barely moves day to day
Its shares cost only a few dollars
questions.answer: Easy to trade without moving the price
questions.why: Easy to trade without moving the price. A stock's liquidity is how fast its shares can be bought or sold without a big hit to the price. FINRA adds: at a fair price, when you want to. It is about the shares trading, not the company's cash, a calm price or a cheap one.
questions.lesson_line: Liquid means you can get in and out fast, at a fair price.

wrong.The company holds plenty of cash: That's the company's balance sheet. A stock's liquidity is about how easily its shares trade.
wrong.Its price barely moves day to day: That's a quiet stock, not a liquid one. Liquidity is about how easily shares trade at a fair price.
wrong.Its shares cost only a few dollars: Cheap doesn't mean liquid. Low-priced, low-volume stocks are generally less liquid.

questions.simple: Liquid means you can buy or sell the shares quickly without moving the price much.

questions.q: On a heavy-volume day, more shares usually get bought than sold.
questions.why: False. There is a seller for every buyer, so shares bought always equal shares sold, on any day. Heavy volume means more shares changed hands. It shows how much traded, not which side pushed, and average volume does not predict direction.
questions.lesson_line: Volume tells you how much traded. It doesn't tell you which way the stock goes.
questions.simple: False, because every share bought is a share sold, so buys and sells always match.

questions.q: What is a stock's dollar volume for a day?
choices: The day's price change in dollars
Buys plus sells, times the price
questions.why: Shares traded times the price. S&P Dow Jones Indices works out dollar value traded the same way: the average closing price times the volume. Each traded share counts once. Shares outstanding times the price is market cap, the value of the whole company, not its trading.
questions.lesson_line: Dollar volume is roughly the money that changes hands in a day.

wrong.Shares outstanding times the price: That's market cap, the value of the whole company. Dollar volume uses only the shares that traded.
wrong.The day's price change in dollars: That's the day's change. It says how far price moved, not how much money traded.
wrong.Buys plus sells, times the price: That counts each share twice. Every share has a buyer and a seller, and volume counts it once.

questions.simple: Dollar volume is the shares traded times the price, roughly the money that changed hands that day.

questions.q: A $40 stock averages 2,500,000 shares a day. What is its average daily dollar volume, in millions?
questions.why: $100 million. Dollar volume is shares times price: 2,500,000 shares at $40 is $100 million a day on average. S&P Dow Jones Indices measures dollar value traded the same way, price times volume.
questions.lesson_line: I read volume in dollars. It puts cheap and pricey stocks on the same scale.
questions.simple: It is $100 million, because 2,500,000 shares times $40 a share is $100 million.

questions.q: A stock averages 1.2 million shares a day. Today it trades 4.8 million. How many times its average is that?
questions.why: 4x. Divide today's volume by the average: 4.8 million over 1.2 million is 4. Measured against the stock's own average, today is clearly heavy. Knowing volume is above average gives a sense of how much conviction a move might have.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy or light is relative. Measure today against the stock's own average.
questions.simple: It is 4 times the average, because 4.8 million divided by 1.2 million is 4.

questions.story: A stock's 50-day average volume is 800,000 shares. This week it trades 760,000 on Monday, 840,000 on Tuesday, 2,400,000 on Wednesday and 910,000 on Thursday.
questions.q: Which day stands out as heavy volume?
questions.why: Wednesday. Judge each day against the 800,000 average. Wednesday's 2,400,000 is far above it. Monday's 760,000, Tuesday's 840,000 and Thursday's 910,000 all sit close to normal. Volume spikes usually come on earnings, a report or news.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy day stands out against the stock's own average.

wrong.Monday: 760,000 is a touch under the 800,000 average. That's a normal day.
wrong.Tuesday: 840,000 is only a touch over the average. Nothing stands out.
wrong.Thursday: 910,000 is a little above average, but nowhere near Wednesday.

questions.simple: Wednesday, because its 2,400,000 shares are far above the 800,000 average, while the other days sit near it.

deeper.counter: Thursday's 910,000 is the highest of the three normal days. Against the 800,000 average it is only a little above, an ordinary day. Wednesday's 2,400,000 is the one far above the average.

questions.q: You want to buy 20,000 shares. The stock averages 80,000 shares a day. What percent of a normal day is your order?
questions.why: 25%. Divide your order by the average day: 20,000 over 80,000 is a quarter of a normal day's volume. Traders often use average volume as a benchmark for trade size. A large order in a low-volume stock can be hard to fill quickly without moving the price. Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. This order is far past it.
questions.lesson_line: Size your order against the average volume. A big slice of the day can move the price on you.
questions.simple: It is 25%, because 20,000 shares is a quarter of the 80,000 shares a normal day trades.

questions.story: Two stocks both quote a one-cent spread. Stock A trades about 10 million shares a day. Stock B trades about 5,000 shares a day.
questions.q: You want to buy 5,000 shares. Which stock takes your order more easily?
choices: Stock A, it trades far more
Stock B, the order is small
questions.answer: Stock A, it trades far more
questions.why: Stock A. Matching spreads don't make two stocks equally liquid, because a narrow spread is not the complete picture. Your 5,000 shares barely register in A's 10 million a day, but they are a full normal day in B. You do better with high volume and a tight spread together.
questions.lesson_line: The spread says what it costs to cross. The volume says how much the stock can take.

wrong.Same, the spreads match: Spreads can be tight on both, which fools people into thinking both are equally liquid.
wrong.Stock B, the order is small: 5,000 shares is not small here. It is a whole normal day in B, so you'll likely move the price getting filled.
wrong.Can't tell without the prices: Your order is counted in shares, so compare shares. 5,000 barely registers against 10 million but is a full day in B.

questions.simple: Stock A, because 5,000 shares is tiny next to its 10 million a day but a full day in B.

deeper.trap: The spread shows only the gap between the best bid and ask right now. It says nothing about how many shares the stock trades in a day. Two names can both quote a one-cent spread while one trades millions of shares and the other a handful. Check both before you size.

questions.story: Stock A trades 3,000,000 shares a day at $2. Stock B trades 400,000 shares a day at $150.
questions.q: Which one trades more dollars each day?
questions.why: B, at $60 million a day. Dollar volume is shares traded times the price. B's 400,000 shares at $150 is $60 million. A trades more shares, but at $2 each they come to far fewer dollars. Compare stocks in dollars traded, not shares.
questions.lesson_line: Compare stocks in dollars traded, not shares. A share count hides the price.

wrong.A, 3 million shares a day: More shares, but cheap ones. At $2 a share, A trades far fewer dollars than B.
wrong.Same, about $6 million each: Not the same. Work out each one: A's cheap shares come to far fewer dollars than B's $60 million.
wrong.Need market cap to tell: Market cap uses shares outstanding. Dollars traded uses only the shares that trade: price times volume.

questions.simple: B trades more dollars, because 400,000 shares at $150 is $60 million a day, while A's cheap shares come to far less.

reasons: fixed before (key was the only dollar choice)

questions.story: You hold 6,000 shares of a small stock that trades about 15,000 shares a day. You decide to sell all of it right now.
questions.q: What should you be ready for?
choices: Taking a lower price to get out
Getting out at the last price
A better price for selling in bulk
questions.answer: Taking a lower price to get out
questions.why: Taking a lower price to get out. Your 6,000 shares are a big slice of a 15,000-share day. In a thin stock, selling quickly can mean accepting a lower price, and any size trade can move the price a lot. Sometimes nobody will buy at a price you'd accept. The last trade is not a promised price.
questions.lesson_line: In a thin stock, the exit is the hard part. Plan it before you buy.

wrong.Getting out at the last price: The last price is a trade that already happened. It is not the price your order is promised.
wrong.Filling all 6,000 at one price: Not in a thin stock. When one price lacks enough shares, parts of a big market order can fill at other prices.
wrong.A better price for selling in bulk: There is no bulk bonus. In a low-volume stock any size trade can move the price a lot, and selling fast can mean a lower price.

questions.simple: Expect a lower price, because a thin stock may lack the buyers to take 6,000 shares fast.

deeper.trap: The trap is planning only the way in. In a thin stock, getting out of a big position is the hard part. Our rule guards against it: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and illiquid stocks are not even watched.

questions.story: The Nasdaq-100 once required an average of 200,000 shares traded a day. Nasdaq noted its members ranged from about $5 to $2,800 a share.
questions.q: Measured in dollars, which stock faced the higher bar under that rule?
questions.why: The $2,800 stock. The old rule counted shares: an average of 200,000 a day. Nasdaq said that, in dollar terms, this was more stringent on high-priced stocks and less on cheap ones. The same share count is far more money at $2,800 than at $5. Nasdaq's current rule uses dollars: at least $5 million a day, on a three-month average.
questions.lesson_line: Same shares, different dollars. That's why I check dollar volume, not just the share count.

wrong.The $5 stock: At $5, 200,000 shares is little money. That was the easy bar to clear.
wrong.Same bar for both: Same share count, very different dollars. Nasdaq pointed to exactly that gap.
wrong.The bigger company: The test counted shares traded, not company size. At the same share count, a higher price means more dollars.

questions.simple: The $2,800 stock, because 200,000 shares at that price is far more money than 200,000 shares at $5.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a share count as a size. 200,000 shares a day sounds the same for every stock. But at $5 it is a small sum, and at $2,800 a huge one. That gap is why Nasdaq's current test is in dollars. It is an index entry rule, not ours: we trade only stocks that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: rule changed over time (Nasdaq-100 liquidity test, re-read 2026-11-12)

questions.q: Thin, low-priced stocks are easier for bad actors to push around.
questions.why: True. FINRA warns that bad actors target stocks with low trading volume and a price of $5 or less. Little public information plus low volume can make an OTC stock's price easier to manipulate. In thin stocks, even fairly small trades can move the price. That does not make every cheap stock a scheme. It means treat sharp spikes there with caution.
questions.lesson_line: Thin, cheap stocks are easier to push around. Treat sudden spikes there with caution.
questions.simple: True, because in a thin, cheap stock even small trades can move the price, which makes it easier to push around.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a sudden spike in a thin, cheap stock as real demand. Even fairly small trades can move these stocks a lot. FINRA says to treat small caps and sharp price spikes and drops with particular caution.

questions.story: A stock usually trades about 2 million shares a day. News hits, and today it trades 14 million. You plan to buy it tomorrow.
questions.q: Which volume should cap the size of your buy?
questions.why: The usual 2 million a day. Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Today's 14 million is one day, not the average. Any single day can trade far above the average, and volume spikes usually come on earnings, reports or news. So cap your size by the average day, not the news day.
questions.lesson_line: Cap your size by the average day, not the news day.

wrong.Today's 14 million shares: That's one news day. A single day can trade far above the stock's average.
wrong.Neither, volume doesn't cap it: It does. Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
wrong.Tomorrow's volume, when you buy: That's one day too, and you can't know it before you buy. Our rule caps you at 1% of the average day.

questions.simple: The usual 2 million a day, because our cap is 1% of the average day, and one news day runs far above it.

deeper.trap: The trap is sizing off the news day. Our rule caps you at 1% of the average day. Any single day can run far above the average, so size from the average, not from one 14 million day.

reasons: the owner's rulebook speaks here (B23, D42: thin stocks are not traded)

questions.q: When markets get rough, thin stocks can get even harder to sell.
questions.why: True. FINRA notes that in a crisis or a volatile market, investors often seek lower-risk assets. That might draw interest to the most liquid securities, while illiquid ones might become even less liquid. Thin stocks can be hard to sell in calm times too, so a selloff can make a hard exit harder.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity can dry up when you need it most. Thin names can get thinner in a selloff.
questions.simple: True, because in rough markets interest can shift to the most liquid stocks, and thin ones can become even less liquid.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging an exit by a calm day. A thin stock you could sell on a quiet afternoon can become even less liquid when the whole market is under stress. Plan the exit for the bad day, not the good one.

questions.story: You want a $60,000 position. Stock X is $12 and averages 25,000 shares a day. Stock Y is $45 and averages 2,000,000 shares a day.
questions.q: Which one can take your size and still let you out cleanly?
questions.why: Stock Y. Multiply price by average volume to see the dollars a stock trades each day. X at $12 on 25,000 shares trades so few dollars that your $60,000 would be a big piece of its day. Y at $45 on 2,000,000 shares trades so much that yours barely shows. A lower share price does not make a stock easier to trade. Our own rule agrees: we trade only stocks that trade at least $20 million a day, and X falls far short.
questions.lesson_line: Before I size up, I check dollar volume. My order should be a small part of a normal day.

wrong.Stock X, it's cheaper: A lower price doesn't make it liquid. X's dollar volume is small, so your order would be a big part of its day.
wrong.Either one at this size: Not here. In X, an order this big against the day's volume can be hard to fill fast without moving the price.
wrong.Neither, $60,000 is too big: Not for Y. It trades millions of shares a day, so your order barely shows there.

questions.simple: Stock Y, because it trades far more dollars a day, so your $60,000 is a tiny part of its normal day.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking the cheaper stock is easier because you get more shares for the money. Price does not decide liquidity; how much trades each day says far more. Before you size up, check what part of a normal day your order would be.

reasons: the owner's rulebook speaks here (B23, D42)

questions.story: You want to sell 3,000 shares of a thin stock. The last trade was $8.40. The best bid is $8.05, with only 300 shares there.
questions.q: Which order fits?
choices: A limit order at a price you accept
A stop order below the bid
questions.answer: A limit order at a price you accept
questions.why: A limit order at a price you accept. In a thin market it keeps you from taking an unwanted price, though it may not fill all at once.
questions.lesson_line: In a thin stock, name your price. A market order lets the thin bids name it for you.

wrong.A market order for all 3,000: Only 300 shares are bid at $8.05. Parts of a big market order fill at other prices, and here that means lower.
wrong.A stop order below the bid: A stop turns into a market order when it triggers. Same problem, just later, and the fill can land far from your stop.

questions.q: A major-exchange listing tells you a stock trades plenty of shares.
questions.why: False. A listing on a major exchange does not promise volume. FINRA warns that bad actors exploit the sense of safety a listing gives. They particularly target listed stocks with low trading volume and a price of $5 or less. Check the average volume yourself before you trust a name.
questions.lesson_line: A listing is not liquidity. Check the average volume before you trust a name.
questions.simple: False, because listed stocks can trade thinly too, so check the volume yourself.

deeper.trap: A big-exchange ticker can feel safe. FINRA's warning is about exactly that feeling: bad actors target listed stocks with low trading volume. The listing tells you where a stock trades, not how much it trades.

reasons: fixed before (why hedged to FINRA's wording)

questions.story: Our rule: trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. A $15 stock averages 500,000 shares a day.
questions.q: What does our rule say about this stock?
choices: We skip it: too few dollars a day
We trade it: price is over $10
We trade it at small size
We skip it until price is $20
questions.answer: We skip it: too few dollars a day
questions.why: We skip it. Our rule needs both lines: a price of $10 or more and at least $20 million traded a day. Price times volume here, $15 times 500,000 shares, is far under $20 million. The price passes; the dollars traded do not.
questions.simple: We skip it, because $15 times 500,000 shares is far less than the $20 million a day our rule needs.
questions.lesson_line: We trade only stocks that clear both lines: $10 a share and $20 million a day.

deeper.trap: The trap is checking only the price. A stock can clear $10 a share and still trade too few dollars a day. Multiply the price by the average volume before a name goes on your list.

wrong.We trade it: price is over $10: The price passes, but our rule needs both lines. At $15, 500,000 shares a day is far under $20 million.
wrong.We trade it at small size: Size can't fix it. The $20 million line decides which stocks we trade at all, and illiquid stocks are not even watched.
wrong.We skip it until price is $20: The $20 million is dollars traded a day, not the share price. Our price line is $10, and $15 already clears it.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. It averages 600,000 shares a day. What is the most we'd own?
questions.why: 6,000 shares. One percent of 600,000 is 6,000. Our rule: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. That keeps our position a tiny part of a normal day, and illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.simple: 6,000 shares, because 1% of the 600,000 shares it trades on an average day is 6,000.
questions.lesson_line: We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (D42)
